text: With any luck my screen will share. Okay can you see that? Yes. Okay so we've been talking about this in oversight I'm sorry community planning and transportation committee in July and August. A number of cities are across the country in dealing with COVID closures began to expand their dining areas out into the public rights of way sidewalks parking spaces those kind of things and so we started looking at this a couple of months ago. This is the kind of stuff we've been talking about. Obviously you have some barrier there to protect the public from sitting and dining public from the traveling public. Different cities doing it different ways but all providing for some protection. We looked primarily at Boulder Fort Collins and Stillwater at their permits and discussing what we might do here and essentially what they've done is they've created a permit called a temporary outdoor extension permit that would allow these restaurants bars and in some cities other uses to expand into the public rights of way and private spaces. Sometimes in some of these cities they were shutting down not just restaurants and bars but retail was really affected and so this was one way they early on kind of addressed some of those issues in the more harder hit areas. Generally speaking all three cities have issued revocable permits meaning if you don't follow the guidelines or the instructions that permit can be taken back at any time. They're issued at the staff level and they're evaluated primarily on public health safety and welfare of course. In some of these policies you see a balance of the needs of the commercial uses with the needs of the surrounding property owners who may be impacted by this. Adequate access is huge through the area around the area and those kind of things. What kind of hours of operation and some cities have imposed a sort of a shutdown time and made that a part of their permit. It has to be immediately adjacent to the place of business in Oklahoma. See similar rules in other cities but in Oklahoma particularly with the able commission this is something that they require but the goal is really to give these places additional capacity without sacrificing social distancing. We have a couple of processes in place already that deal with with certain types of events. The special events ordinance deals with large events, game day, music festival, things like that. Things that are anticipated to be open for at least two hours open to the public with a thousand or more people anticipated to attend and that allows for street closures, barricades and such to help operate the special event area. That's not something that's practical for everyday use but it does kind of give us some guidance for this use. We also have parking variances that we grant from time to time. Those go through the police department and we have to make sure you're allowing pedestrian and emergency vehicle access but again those are short term not something that would become a regular part of the business and so they they don't really fit for this. Recently we've really pushed sidewalk dining. We have a permit process that allows restaurants to serve food outside adjacent to the business. A tough sell in the summer in Oklahoma probably for some. You have to maintain public access across the sidewalk and so that can be difficult. You have to be in an area where the sidewalks are wide enough to accommodate both your outdoor seating and the passage of the public. So in looking at a temporary outdoor expansion permit we have to consider safety obviously. We want the pedestrian access to continue to be accessible. We want the dining areas to be protected from traffic. We want to think about the loss of public parking. If this were to really grow that's probably something we'd want to consider. The licensing as I said the able license particularly requires that this be done adjacent to the licensed premise and so how does that work when you have a sidewalk right there that you need to maintain access on and then coordination with adjacent properties. So what I have drafted is a proposed proclamation that could be done by the mayor at any time but I know that it was really important to her that we get feedback on this and not just adopt it and it follows a similar process to these other cities. A revocable permit so a permit that would be granted based on eligibility following all the application guidelines and the rules and then it could be revoked if those rules weren't followed. To be eligible you have to operate a permanent location within Norman. This makes sense for a number of reasons but able regulations being one of them if this isn't really an ordinance or a proclamation that works well with things like food trucks that are that are mobile and they don't have a permanent location. You have to show proof of all applicable licenses so if you need a license from the health department if you need a license from the city to operate as a restaurant if you need your able licenses all those need to be current before you could get this kind of permit. Insurance is a big one because they are going to be operating in our public rights of way that we we control and that we can be liable for and so we want the city to be named as an additional insured on their insurance policy and it needs to at least be in the limits that the governmental court claims act says we can be liable for. With their application they would be including a sketch of the proposed expanded service area where are those barriers where do you propose the tables go how do people get into the barricaded area and how do people get around so if you're using the whole sidewalk and into the parking area something Stillwater did is they had to show a barricaded sidewalk area wide enough for ADA accessibility around the dining area. Safety barriers obviously this is a key component we want people to be safe when they're sitting out there and so these barriers may differ based on whether they're in a private parking lot where there's not traffic or whether they're in you know on main street where the traffic's going by at a pretty quick pace sometimes and all that's just based on safety. Design and operation of course this is to enable social distancing not to enable more crowds necessarily we want to get more occupancy more capacity without sacrificing that social distancing so the tables have to be arranged in the barricaded area six feet apart and then they have to be able if it's a bar to deny access to non-customers bar or restaurant and then under 21 obviously if it's a bar. This also is written to allow for staff approval it's the way it's written now it goes to the city manager after review by public works the planning department the police department to make sure that it's it's meeting all these public safety requirements. It would expire right there with our mask ordinance on November 30th unless it's modified or extended or even rescinded if things really turn around and we want to open back up so with that I'm happy to answer any questions. I'll take your feedback and work that into the final draft before presenting it to the mayor.
